speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I want to explain a result that most students find annoying. If you read a chapter twice, you will feel that you know it. If instead you read it once and then close the book and write down everything you can remember, you will feel considerably worse. You will also, two weeks later, remember roughly twice as much. The reason is that retrieval is not a test of learning. It is an episode of learning. Each time you pull a fact out of memory, the route to that fact is strengthened, in a way that simply seeing the fact again does not strengthen it. So the discomfort you feel is not a sign that the method is failing. It is a sign that the method is doing the work. There is a catch, and it matters. Retrieval only helps if you afterwards check what you got wrong. Students who test themselves and never look at the answers improve very little, because they rehearse their errors as faithfully as their successes. So the sequence is: read once, close the book, write what you have, and then — this is the part people skip — go back and find out which parts you invented.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: Last week I told you when to study. Today I want to tell you what order to study in, because that answer is also counterintuitive. Suppose you have three topics to revise. The natural approach is to finish the first, then the second, then the third. Psychologists call that blocking. The alternative is to move between them — a little of the first, a little of the third, back to the second — which is called interleaving. Blocking feels far better. While you are inside one topic everything connects, each problem resembles the last, and you get faster. Interleaving feels like being interrupted. And yet, across studies in mathematics, in medical diagnosis, even in identifying painters by their style, the interleaved groups perform worse during practice and substantially better on the test. The reason is that blocking lets you stop choosing. When every problem on the page is the same kind, you never have to work out which method applies; you only have to apply it. The examination, of course, does not tell you which method applies. That is most of what it is testing. Interleaving puts the choosing back in. One caution. Interleaving helps between things that could be confused with each other. Alternating between statistics and Spanish is simply task-switching, and that costs you.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: People often picture a climate model as a very large piece of software that is asked what the temperature will be in 2080. That is not what it does. A model divides the atmosphere and the ocean into boxes, and for each box it applies the same physics you would apply to a bucket of air: conservation of energy, conservation of mass, the behaviour of water as it changes state. Then it steps forward, half an hour at a time, for a simulated century. Nothing in that process is a prediction. The model is told what the emissions are; it is not asked to guess them. So when two models disagree, it is worth asking which kind of disagreement it is. If they were given different emissions, they are answering different questions and the gap means very little. If they were given identical emissions and still differ, the gap is telling you something about the physics they represent differently, and clouds are almost always where that difference lives. That second kind is the interesting one, and it is the one that has narrowed slowly over thirty years.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I want to spend ten minutes on four words, because they are the four most misread words this field publishes. When a report says something is virtually certain, it means a probability above ninety-nine per cent. Very likely means above ninety. Likely means above sixty-six. And more likely than not means above fifty. Those are definitions, not impressions, and they are printed in a table at the front of the report. What happens next is entirely predictable. A newspaper reads likely and writes may. May has no number attached to it at all; it is compatible with one per cent and with ninety-nine. So a statement with a defined floor of two thirds becomes a statement with no floor, and nobody has told a lie. The second thing that happens is the reverse. A finding reported as more likely than not, which is barely better than a coin toss, gets reported as a finding, full stop, and the hedge simply disappears. If you take one thing from this hour, take this. When you meet one of those four phrases, go and find the table that defines it. It is always there, and almost nobody looks at it.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I want to take apart a sentence you will meet constantly, which is that a species adapted to its environment. The sentence is not wrong, but it hides the mechanism, and the hidden part is where most people go astray. Consider a population of birds in which beak depth varies, as it does in every real population. A drought arrives and the only seeds left are large and hard. Birds with deeper beaks crack them; birds with shallower beaks do not, and many of those birds die. The survivors breed, and because beak depth is heritable, the next generation has on average a slightly deeper beak than the generation before the drought. Notice what did not happen. No bird grew a deeper beak. No bird tried harder. The variation was already present before the drought began, and all the drought did was change which portion of it was passed on. This is why the phrase adapted to is best read as a description of an outcome rather than an account of a process. The process is differential survival acting on variation that already exists, and if you can hold those two ideas together you will not be caught by most of the confusions in this field.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: Last week I gave you the finch result and said it was the clearest demonstration of selection ever recorded. Today I want to say why that sentence needs a second half. The study was done on one small island, over thirty years, by one team. Every one of those is a strength and a limit at the same time. One island means the conditions were simple enough to measure, and it also means we do not know whether the same thing happens where the food is varied. Thirty years means the slow changes are visible, and it also means we have one long run rather than several independent ones. One team means the methods were consistent, and it also means that if the team had a systematic habit, it is in every year of the data. None of this makes the result weaker. It makes it a result about one place, which is what every result is until somebody repeats it somewhere else. The honest sentence is not that selection works like this, but that on this island, over this period, measured this way, it did.

text: I would take the repeat. A large study can be large and still wrong in one consistent way, because everything in it shares a method, a place and a season. speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: There is a habit of mind I want you to resist, and it is the habit of asking who got there first. The question feels natural and it produces bad archaeology, because it makes every site a competitor and every date a claim to a title. A better question is what the distribution of dates looks like. If the earliest secure sites cluster along a coast and the inland corridor sites are consistently later, that pattern tells you something about a route. It tells you more than any single early date could, and it is far harder to overturn, because it does not rest on one excavation being right. Now, the uncomfortable part. We have known for decades that radiocarbon dates from coastal sites are harder to interpret, because marine carbon behaves differently from atmospheric carbon. That is not a reason to discard them. It is a reason to correct them, and to say in the paper exactly what correction was applied. A date without its correction stated is not a measurement; it is an assertion. And a field that publishes assertions will eventually find itself arguing about who got there first, which is where we came in.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: Here is a question that sounds pedantic and is not. When a laboratory gives you a date of eleven thousand years, what is eleven thousand years old? The answer is the sample. Not the fire, not the camp, not the people. The sample. If the sample is a piece of charcoal from a tree that was already two hundred years old when it was cut, then the outer rings died when it was cut and the inner rings died two centuries earlier, and which part went to the laboratory matters enormously. If it was driftwood, the tree may have died on another coast entirely, long before anyone picked it up. This is called the old wood problem, and the uncomfortable thing about it is that it never shows up in the number. The laboratory reports exactly what it measured, with an honest uncertainty, and the uncertainty is about the measurement. It is not about your inference. So when you read a site report, do not stop at the date. Find the sentence that says what was dated and where it was lying, and if that sentence is missing, treat the date as a claim rather than as a measurement.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I am often asked why so much of what we do in space is done without people, and the honest answer has three parts. The first is duration. A probe can wait. It can spend seven years travelling to a planet and then work for twenty more, and it does not need to be fed or brought home. No crewed mission has ever been designed on that timescale, and none realistically could be. The second is mass. Every kilogram of life support is a kilogram not spent on instruments, and the ratio is brutal: a crewed vehicle carries a small fraction of the scientific payload that an uncrewed one of the same mass can carry. The third part is the one people like least. It is risk. We have lost a great many spacecraft and we will lose more, and that is an acceptable cost precisely because nobody is aboard. Now, I want to be careful here, because this is not an argument that people should never go. There are things a geologist standing on a surface can do in an afternoon that a rover has not managed in a decade. But if the question is where the knowledge has come from so far, the answer is overwhelmingly from machines that went alone.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: You will read the word candidate a great deal this term, and I want you to understand that it is not a hedge. It is a decision. Any method that looks for faint signals has to put a line somewhere, and wherever the line goes it creates two kinds of mistake. Put it low and you will catch every real object and also some things that are not objects at all. Put it high and you will throw away real ones. There is no setting that avoids both, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. Now, which mistake would you rather make? This field has mostly chosen to risk missing things, and the reason is not statistical. It is about what happens afterwards. A false detection gets announced, repeated, built on, and then quietly withdrawn two years later, and the withdrawal reaches perhaps a tenth of the people the announcement reached. A missed planet is usually found by somebody else within a few years, and the embarrassment is confined to one team. So when a paper says candidate about an object the authors are privately confident in, they are not being coy. They are telling you which of those two futures they decided to risk.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I want to spend a few minutes on a word that causes more trouble than any other in this subject, and that word is metabolism. People speak of having a fast metabolism or a slow one, as though it were a single dial that could be turned up. It is not one process. It is the sum of every chemical conversion going on in the body at once, and the great majority of them are not optional. Keeping your heart beating, your temperature steady and your cell membranes intact accounts for most of what you spend in a day. Deliberate activity accounts for far less than people expect. Now, this matters practically. If you take in less than you spend, the body does not simply draw the difference from stored fat and carry on as before. It also reduces what it spends, quietly, by lowering body temperature slightly, by moving less, by making a hundred small economies you do not notice and cannot feel. This is why the arithmetic that looks so simple on paper behaves so badly in practice, and why anyone who tells you the sum is straightforward has not looked at the measurements.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: Everybody in this room can recite the energy equation. Intake minus expenditure equals change in storage. It is true. It is also, as a tool for predicting anything, close to useless, and I want to be precise about why. The reason is not that the equation is wrong. The reason is that the two terms are not independent of each other. Reduce intake and expenditure falls as well, partly for an uninteresting reason and partly for an interesting one. The uninteresting reason is that a lighter body costs less to carry about, so the same walk uses less energy than it did. The interesting reason is regulation. Core temperature drops very slightly. Spontaneous movement falls, and nobody notices themselves fidgeting less. These are not decisions. Nobody chooses them and nobody feels them. So when a prediction built on the static equation says a particular reduction will produce a particular loss over six months, the prediction is almost always too large, and the error is not small. None of this means intake does not matter. It means an equation whose two sides are tied together cannot be solved as though they were free.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: There is a sentence I want you to be suspicious of whenever you meet it, and it is that the market will decide. The market is not a person and it does not decide anything. What exists is a very large number of people, each responding to the prices and rules they face, and the pattern that results. Saying that the market decided is a way of describing an outcome without naming anyone responsible for the rules that produced it. Take a congestion charge. If you price entry to a city centre, traffic falls. That is not the market deciding; that is a specific rule, set by a specific body, having a predictable effect. If the charge is set too low, traffic does not fall and the scheme is called a failure of the market, when it was a failure of the price. The reason this matters to you is that almost every economic argument you will read contains at least one sentence of this kind. When you find it, ask who set the rule, and what they were trying to achieve. The answer is usually available and usually interesting.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: Last week I asked you to be suspicious of the sentence that the market will decide. Today I want to take one rule and ask who it lands on. A congestion charge of five pounds. It is the same five pounds for everybody, which sounds like fairness and is not. For a household with very little spare income, five pounds a day is a prohibition. For a household with a great deal, it is a parking fee and barely noticed. Now hold those two facts together, because the consequence is uncomfortable. The traffic reduction the scheme reports comes almost entirely from the first household. The second one is still driving. So the scheme achieves its target by changing the behaviour of the people least able to absorb it, and the benefit — the quieter street, the cleaner air — is enjoyed most by the people who did not change. text: I want to show you why a single number can be entirely accurate and still mislead almost everyone who reads it. Consider a disease that kills one per cent of the people who catch it. speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: When you look at a map of a city you are looking at a decision, although it rarely announces itself as one. Streets do not arrange themselves. Somebody decided how wide they would be, who would pay for them, and what would be demolished to make room. Consider the grid. A grid is often described as the natural form of a city, and it is nothing of the kind. It is a form that makes land easy to survey, easy to divide and easy to sell, which is why it appears wherever land was being distributed quickly. The curving streets of an older European quarter are not a different aesthetic; they are the record of a different process, in which the street followed the boundary of whatever was already there. Now, why does this matter when you are reading about transport? Because the argument you will meet most often is that a city is congested because it was badly planned. Sometimes that is true. More often the city was planned for a different purpose, by people with different instruments, and what you are looking at is not a failure but an inheritance.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: Last week I said a map is a decision. Today I want to show you a number that is also a decision, and it is the one that decides which transport schemes get built. The number is time saved. You take the journeys people currently make along a corridor, you work out how much quicker each would be after the scheme, you multiply by a value per hour, and you compare that with the cost. It is a perfectly reasonable thing to compute. Now ask yourself who is in that calculation. Everyone who already makes the journey. And who is not? The person who cannot cross the road on foot and therefore makes no journey at all. The child who is not allowed to walk to school. Neither of them has a journey time, because neither of them has a journey, so neither contributes a single minute to the total. The measure is not biased because somebody wanted it to be. It is biased because of what it is made of: it counts the journeys the network already permits, which is exactly the set of journeys that needs the least help. And a measure like that will recommend making easy journeys easier, forever, and it will do it with impeccable arithmetic.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I want to put a question to you that sounds simple and is not. Should a rule ever be broken? The usual classroom answer is that it depends on the rule, which is true and almost useless, so let us be more precise. There is a difference between a rule you think is wrong and a rule you think does not apply to you. Breaking a rule you believe is unjust, openly, and accepting the penalty, is a recognised political act with a long history. Breaking the same rule quietly, because it is inconvenient, is not that act, even when the rule is equally unjust and the person equally sincere. The difference is not in the rule and it is not in the motive. It is in whether you are trying to change the rule or trying to escape it. And notice what follows. Accepting the penalty is not a moral flourish. It is the thing that makes the act legible as an argument rather than as an evasion. Take that away and the observer cannot tell the two cases apart, which means the act can no longer do the work it was meant to do.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: Here are two reports of the same afternoon. The first begins with eleven arrests. The second begins with four thousand people. Both numbers appear in both reports. Nothing has been invented and nothing has been omitted. And yet a reader of the first comes away with a disturbance, and a reader of the second with a demonstration. So where did that come from? Two places, and neither of them is a lie. The first is order. Whatever stands at the top of a report is what the report is about, and deciding what goes first is a judgement about what matters, made by somebody, usually in a hurry. The second is the verb. A crowd that clashed with police has done something. A crowd that was dispersed by police has had something done to it. Same afternoon, and the agent has moved from one side of the sentence to the other. Now, I am not telling you both reports are equally good. I am telling you that you cannot settle which is better by checking the facts, because the facts are not where the disagreement is. You settle it by asking what each report decided to put first, and why.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I am going to defend a sentence that students are often told to avoid, which is the passive. You will have been advised to write the researchers heated the sample rather than the sample was heated, on the grounds that the active is clearer. In most writing that advice is sound. In a methods section it is wrong, and for a reason worth understanding. A methods section is a set of instructions for reproducing what was done. Who did it is, for that purpose, irrelevant. If the result depends on which person held the pipette, you have not described a method; you have described an anecdote. The passive removes the agent precisely because the agent should not matter, and the sentence is honest about that. Now, the passive is also used to hide agency when agency is exactly what a reader needs, and that is a real abuse. Mistakes were made is the famous example. The test is simple enough: ask whether naming the agent would change what a competent reader should do next. In a methods section it would not. In an apology it would.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: You have all read that a large proportion of published findings do not replicate, and the usual reaction is to conclude that researchers are careless. I want to persuade you that this is the least interesting explanation available, and almost certainly wrong. Ask instead who is paid to check. Appointments are made on original findings. Grants are awarded for new questions. Promotion panels count papers, and a replication is either not a paper at all, because the journal declined it, or it is a paper that adds nothing to your record and makes an enemy of somebody in your field. Now, none of that requires anybody to behave badly. A researcher who spends a year carefully checking somebody else's claim has spent a year that counts for nothing, whichever way the check comes out. That is not carelessness. That is a system doing exactly what it is arranged to do. And it tells you why the remedies being adopted are procedural rather than moral: registering analyses in advance, requiring materials to be shared, accepting papers on the method before the results exist. Each of those takes a decision away from the moment where the incentive is strongest. Exhortation has been tried for about a century, and the record is not encouraging.

speaker: You
text: I would start with what kind of claim it is. speaker: Dan Okafor

speaker: You
text: I would have journals accept papers on the method alone, before the results exist. The reason is that every other reform depends on people behaving well, and this one does not: if acceptance is decided before anyone knows what was found, the result stops being the thing the work is aimed at. The cost is real and I would not pretend otherwise. Editors judging a method blind will be cautious, and the literature would fill up with careful studies of safe questions. I still think that is a better failure than the one we have.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I want to talk about a habit of reading that will serve you in every subject, and it is the habit of separating what a writer claims from what a writer has shown. Criticism is unusually good practice for this, because critics tend to move between the two without marking the transition. Here is a typical sentence. The film refuses the consolations of its genre, choosing instead to leave its audience unsettled. Now, part of that is observation. The film does not end the way films of that kind usually end, and anyone can check it. The rest is interpretation. Refusing is a word about intention, and choosing is another, and neither of them is visible on the screen. I am not objecting to the sentence. Interpretation is the whole point of criticism and a review without it would be a listing. What I am asking is that you notice where the joint is. When you meet a claim about what a work is doing, ask what you would have to see in order to agree, and then ask whether the writer has shown you that. Sometimes they have. When they have not, you have found the place where the argument is actually being made.

speaker: Professor Nadia Haddad
text: I want to end on a question that is asked badly almost every time it is asked. Does the audience change the work? There are two claims hiding inside that sentence, and they are not the same claim. The first is that different people have different experiences of the same work, and that somebody who knows the tradition sees things a newcomer does not. That is obviously true. Nobody has ever seriously denied it, and an essay that spends two thousand words establishing it has established nothing. The second claim is that the work itself is different — that there is no object sitting underneath all these experiences, only the experiences. That is a real position, it has serious people on both sides, and it is hard. Now, what happens in practice is that an essay argues for the first claim, which is easy, and concludes the second, which is not. The move is almost never deliberate. It happens because the same sentence can express both, and English is quite happy to let it. So when you read this argument, and you will read it often, find the sentence where the writer slides from one to the other. It is usually a single word, and it is usually a verb.

text: Describe a book, film or piece of music that changed your mind about something. Be specific about what did it.

speaker: You
text: A documentary about an orchestra changed how I listen. There is a sequence where the same two minutes are played three times: once by the full orchestra, once by the strings alone, and once by a single player. Nothing is explained over it. What changed for me was that I could finally hear what a part contributes, because I had heard the same passage with it and without it. Before that I had been told music was layered and had never actually perceived the layers.

speaker: Dan Okafor
text: Does an audience change a work, or only its own experience of it? Give your reasons.

speaker: You
text: I think it changes the experience, and I am not persuaded it changes the work. It is obviously true that a film means something different to someone who knows its tradition and someone who does not — nobody disputes that. The stronger claim is that these are therefore different works, and I resist it because it would make disagreement impossible. When two people argue about an ending they are arguing about the same sequence of shots, and that shared object is exactly what lets them disagree at all.

speaker: Dan Okafor
text: What is one habit of reading or listening you would keep from this course, and why that one?

speaker: You
text: Asking what I would have to see in order to agree. It sounds like a small thing and it does most of the work of the others. It is the same question as asking what a rate was divided by, or what a chart was computed from, or which claim a sentence is actually making — all of those turned out to be one habit wearing different clothes. What I like about it is that it is not scepticism. It does not ask whether something is true. It asks what would settle it, which is a question you can answer, and often the answer is already on the page.
